topic: Advanced Graph - Bridges, Articulation Points, SCC

sections.title: What is Advanced Graph Analysis?
sections.content:
Advanced graph algorithms find the structural weak points and strongly connected regions within a graph. Three concepts are central here: **bridges**, **articulation points**, and **strongly connected components (SCCs)**.

A **bridge** is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components - it is a critical connection with no alternative path around it. A **articulation point** (also called a cut vertex) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph. Together, bridges and articulation points represent the fragile structure of a network: the edges and nodes that, if removed, would fragment it.

A **Strongly Connected Component (SCC)** applies to directed graphs. An SCC is a maximal subset of vertices such that every vertex in the subset is reachable from every other vertex. SCCs reveal the 'islands of mutual reachability' in a directed graph - for instance, in a web graph, all pages that can reach each other through directed links form an SCC.

All three can be computed in O(V + E) using DFS-based algorithms. The key insight across all of them is the concept of **back edges** in a DFS tree and the **low value** - the earliest discovery time reachable from a subtree via at most one back edge. These algorithms appear in network reliability analysis, dependency resolution, circuit design, and social network analysis.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use bridge/articulation point algorithms when the problem asks for edges or nodes whose removal disconnects a network - 'critical connections,' 'critical servers,' '2-edge-connected components,' or network reliability. Use SCC algorithms when the problem involves directed graphs and asks for groups of mutually reachable nodes, condensation of a directed graph, or safe nodes in a directed graph. These algorithms are not needed for simple reachability or shortest-path problems.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## Bridges and Tarjan's Bridge Algorithm

Run DFS and track two values for each node `u`:
- `disc[u]` - the **discovery time** when `u` was first visited (a global timer incremented each visit)
- `low[u]` - the **lowest discovery time reachable** from the subtree rooted at `u` using at most one back edge

Update rules:
- After recursing into child `v` (tree edge): `low[u] = Math.min(low[u], low[v])`
- When `v` is already visited and not the parent (back edge): `low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v])`

An edge `(u, v)` is a **bridge** if `low[v] > disc[u]`. This means `v`'s subtree has no back edge reaching `u` or any ancestor of `u` - the only connection between `v`'s component and the rest is the edge `(u, v)` itself.

**Critical for undirected graphs**: when recursing from `u` into neighbor `v`, skip the edge back to `u`'s parent. Track the parent node explicitly and skip `if (v === parent)`. Without this, the direct parent edge is counted as a back edge and `low[u]` is incorrectly reduced.

## Articulation Points

Similar to bridges but identifies vertices instead of edges. Node `u` is an **articulation point** if either:
1. `u` is the **root** of the DFS tree and has **2 or more children** (removing it disconnects those children)
2. `u` is **not the root** and has a child `v` where `low[v] >= disc[u]` - meaning `v`'s subtree cannot reach any ancestor of `u`, so removing `u` disconnects `v`'s subtree

The difference from bridges: bridges use `low[v] > disc[u]`, articulation points use `low[v] >= disc[u]`.

## Tarjan's SCC Algorithm (Directed Graphs)

Maintains a **stack** of nodes currently in the DFS path (distinct from the `visited` set). Tracks `disc` and `low` values. When `low[u] === disc[u]`, node `u` is the root of an SCC. Pop all nodes from the stack down to and including `u` - they form one SCC.

A node is in the stack if it is part of the current DFS path and its SCC has not yet been finalized. Back edges in directed graphs update `low[u]` only if the neighbor is on the current stack (not just visited - a node already popped belongs to a different, already-finalized SCC).

## Kosaraju's SCC Algorithm

An alternative to Tarjan's using two full DFS passes:
1. DFS on the **original graph**, push each node onto a stack in **finish order** (node is pushed after all its neighbors are processed)
2. **Transpose** the graph (reverse all edge directions)
3. Pop nodes from the stack and DFS on the **transposed graph** in that order. Each DFS tree in pass 2 is one SCC

Conceptually cleaner than Tarjan's. Same O(V + E) complexity. The intuition: the node that finishes last in pass 1 can reach the most nodes; in the transposed graph, it can only be reached from its own SCC.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Implements Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm. For each DFS tree edge (u, v), a bridge is detected when low[v] > disc[u] - meaning v's subtree has no back edge to reach u or above. Returns all bridge edges as [u, v] pairs.

items.name: Articulation Points
items.description: Minor modification to the bridge algorithm. A non-root node u is an articulation point if any child v has `low[v] >= disc[u]`. The root is an articulation point if it has 2+ children in the DFS tree. Track a `children` count for the root separately.

items.name: Tarjan's SCC (Directed)
items.description: Single-pass DFS with a stack to find strongly connected components in a directed graph. When low[u] === disc[u], pop the stack to collect the SCC. A node on the stack is 'in the current path'; a popped node belongs to a finished SCC and must not update low values.

items.name: Kosaraju's SCC
items.description: Two-pass DFS: first pass on original graph records finish order; second pass on transposed graph processes nodes in reverse finish order. Each DFS tree in pass 2 is one SCC. Easier to reason about correctness but requires building the transposed graph.

items.name: Biconnected Components
items.description: Find maximal 2-edge-connected subgraphs (no bridges within them). Uses the same DFS framework - track edges on a stack and pop them when a bridge is found. Each popped group forms a biconnected component.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: All three algorithms (Tarjan's bridge, Tarjan's SCC, Kosaraju's SCC) perform a constant number of DFS traversals. Each DFS visits every vertex once and processes each edge once: O(V + E). Space is O(V + E) for the adjacency list, plus O(V) for the disc, low, visited, and stack arrays. Kosaraju's also builds the transposed graph: O(V + E) additional space.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Bridge algorithm on undirected graphs: not tracking the parent node and skipping the edge back to it - the parent edge looks like a back edge and incorrectly reduces `low[u]`, making real bridges invisible. Always pass `parent` and skip `if (v === parent)`.

Tarjan's SCC requires a stack separate from the visited set - a node can be 'visited' (disc != -1) but already popped from the stack (its SCC is finalized). Back edges should update `low[u]` only if the neighbor is still on the stack, not just visited.
Initializing disc and low to `0` instead of `-1` - using 0 conflates 'unvisited' with 'visited at time 0', causing the algorithm to skip nodes. Always initialize to -1.

Applying SCC algorithms to undirected graphs - SCCs are defined only for directed graphs. On an undirected graph, every connected component is trivially strongly connected. Use simple DFS/BFS for undirected components.

Off-by-one in the timer: using a per-call local timer instead of a shared closure/reference timer - each DFS subtree gets its own time starting at 0, making all disc values equal and breaking all comparisons.

items.title: Critical Connections in a Network
items.why: The canonical bridge-finding problem - direct application of Tarjan's bridge algorithm with disc and low values.

items.title: Find Eventual Safe States
items.why: Tests understanding of directed graph cycle detection and SCC concepts - safe nodes are those not part of or leading into cycles.

items.title: Minimum Number of Days to Disconnect Island
items.why: Tests bridge and articulation point concepts - if the grid has a bridge or articulation point, disconnection requires removing 1 cell instead of 2.

items.title: Strongly Connected Component
items.why: Direct application of Tarjan's SCC or Kosaraju's algorithm - find all SCCs in a directed graph.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: After advanced graph algorithms, the next Level 7 topic is Mo's Algorithm - a completely different domain (offline range queries) that introduces the square-root decomposition paradigm. It broadens your toolkit from graph-based thinking to array query optimization.
